newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stock markets seen awaiting FOMC meeting.
newsitem.headline: Asian stock markets seen awaiting FOMC meeting.

text.p: The tone of trading on Asian stocks markets this week appears certain to be set by whether the United States decides to increase interest rates or not.
Asian markets and Wall Street will be waiting for Tuesday's meeting of the Federal Reserve's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
Many analysts expect a modest increase in short-term interest rates to head off inflationary pressures.
The key Tokyo market is closed on Monday and investors in the region are likely to hold back anyway until the FOMC meeting has re-examined monetary policy.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed 20.72 points higher at 5,888.46, just shy of Monday's all-time high finish of 5,889.20, after hitting 5,897 earlier. For the week, the Dow rose 49.94 points.
TOKYO - Share prices in Tokyo are expected to hover in a 21,000 to 22,000 range, with participants eyeing on the U.S. policymaking meeting on September 24, brokers said.

"Even if the Fed raises its interest rates, Japan is unlikely to tighten its credit stance," said Kenichi Sagami, general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd. But if the Fed's action moves U.S. stocks, "the New York market affects the Tokyo market psychologically", he said.
Masaaki Higashida, deputy general manager of Nomura Securities Co Ltd, said the market lacked factors to inspire buying incentives, although sentiment had improved.
On Friday, the key 225-issue Nikkei average closed down 210.61 points or 0.99 percent at 21,112.24. Its key December futures shed 140 points to 21,180. It closed at 20,842.64 a week earlier.
HONG KONG - Stocks are expected to take their lead from the Fed meeting, sustaining recent gains if U.S. interest rates remain steady but suffering a setback if rates move higher, analysts said.
Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities, said a 25 basis point rise in interest rates had been discounted and would only prompt a temporary fall in prices.
"If it is more than 25 basis points, the immediate reaction will be down 200 or 300 points," he said.
The Hang Seng rose 223.32 points, or 1.96 percent, last week, closing on a gain of 5.68 points on Friday at 11,592.36.
BANGKOK - Analysts expect the market to move slightly higher following Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's announcement that he will resign within seven days.
"The market will react positively on the developments but investors will wait to see how developments unfold," one foreign analyst said.
The market rose briefly near the end of the week on investor anticipation there might be some changes in the government.
The SET index closed at 1045.38 on Friday, compared to 1,039.65 last Friday.
BOMBAY - Indian shares will remain range-bound as market participants watch political developments, brokers said.
Traders expect a long-awaited police report on a bribery scandal involving former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to be submitted to court. Rao has denied involvement in the scandal.
Traders say the report is crucial because the ruling minority coalition government's survival is dependent on support from Rao's Congress party in parliament.
In the week to Friday, the 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index lost 0.59 points to 3,346.78.
COLOMBO - Sri Lankan stocks are expected to start the coming week firmer but could face profit-taking later, brokers said.
"Investors know there are sellers waiting to take profits when the all share reaches about 580 points," said Sanjeeva Gunewardena of Commercial Stock Brokers.
Optimism in plantation shares pushed the index out of the tight groove it had remained in for about a month, brokers said.
The all share index closed on Friday at 572.84, up 10.8 points or 1.9 percent from a week earlier.
DHAKA - Dhaka stocks posted a modest gain over the week in an overall buoyant market which also saw a brief midweek correction, market analysts said.
Brokers expect the market to maintain the uptrend when trading resumes on Saturday after the Friday Moslem weekened.
The Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) index gained 35.16 points to 1,562.66 in the week ending on Thursday.
JAKARTA - Jakarta share prices are expected to move up slightly with both foreign and local operators likely to buy more big- and medium-capitalised stocks.

"The market has acted ahead of the Federal Reserve decision on the U.S. interest rates. I expect foreign buying will continue in selected stocks," Jordan Zulkarnain, analyst of PT Pentasena Securities, said .
Another analyst from a foreign brokerage firm said receding political tension in Jakarta had prompted more foreign buying.
Brokers said local operators were likely to be active with positive corporate actions and rumours as driving factors.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed at 568.99 points, against last week's close of 549.04 points.
KARACHI - Pakistani stocks could take a dive on fears of unrest after the killing of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's estranged brother, dealers said.
Murtaza Bhutto, 42, died after a shootout between his supporters and police in Karachi on Friday night.
The Karachi 100-share index had been poised for a sharp rise on short covering in blue chips, but the killing has added new uncertainty to a turbulent political scene, dealers said.
On Thursday, the index ended 60.07 points, or 4.36 percent, up at 1,438.42 amid 200 gainers and 72 losers, against a rise of 31.99 points, or 2.40 percent, to 1,362.94 on September 12.
KUALA LUMPUR - After weeks of spectacular gains, Malaysia's Second Board stocks are likely to do some retracing.
The shortening of the settlement period and possible tightening of share financing for Second Board stocks will be contributory factors, dealers said.
"We are anticipating the trade figures to be out next week. We feel the deficit should have dropped to around 300 million ringgit," said Stephen Weller, a strategist at Pesaka Jardine Fleming.
Week-on-week, the Composite Index was up 13.05 points at 1130.60, while the Second board index was up 34.89 at 607.13.
MANILA - Manila shares are likely to drift in a narrow range as investors bide their time awaiting more incentives to buy shares, traders said.

Although it is widely expected the market will move up on a technical rally after the Fed meeting on Tuesday, any advance will likely be capped because the market is trading at an expensive level of 20 to 21 times 1996 forecast earnings, said Conrad Andres, research head of DBP-Daiwa Securities.
"Occasional rallies are being seen as opportunities to sell. The market is neither here or there," he said.
The Philippine bourse ended the week 1.5 percent higher from the previous week at 3,242.22 points.
SEOUL - Large-capitalised stocks will continue to be under selling pressure by investors who have to redeem huge margin loans at brokerage houses, brokers said.

But selective buying prior to the October 1 increase in the foreign shareholding limit is expected to help support the index, they said. The market will be closed from Thursday until Sunday for Chusok, the Korean Thanksgiving holidays.
"Concerns about the margin loans will keep depressing the market," said Dongwon Securities broker Choo Hee-yup.
The composite index closed at 759.35 on Friday, down 3.29 percent or 25.84 points from the previous Friday's 785.19.
SINGAPORE - The Singapore share market is seen drifting sideways after buying from funds appeared to have dried up.
"The market will slip back to a cautious position," said a sales director with a foreign brokerage.
He said unexciting local fundamentals have been factored into share prices but unexpected sharp movements in Wall Street could cause adverse reactions in the bourse.
On Friday, the Straits Times Industrials Index ended at 2,187.86, up 61.59 points from the previous week's 2,126.27.
SYDNEY - The Australian share market will be looking for a lead from the United States ahead of the Fed's policy-setting meeting, but metal prices are still key to the market, brokers said.
"The resources are likely to be the stronger influence over the short term as commodity prices are being watched very closely," one Sydney-based broker said.

The All Ordinaries finished at 2,240.8, down 11.5 points over the week, almost ignoring the record highs hit on Wall Street this week. Trading is likely to remain quiet in the absence of significant Australian economic data and following the end of the annual corporate reporting season.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected to stay in a narrow-range consolidation amid caution in front of September 27's Mid Autumn Festival, brokers said.
"Without further bullish news, most people believe the index is unlikely to breach the 6,600-point resistance before the Mid Autumn Festival," said George Hou of Jardine Fleming.
Some investors would continue to sell shares to build liquidity for the holiday and people were also likely to be cautious before the three-day-long weekend.
The index is expected to move between 6,500 and 6,600 points during the week, brokers said. On Friday, it ended at 6,499.52 points, compared with 6,471.63 a week earlier.
WELLINGTON - The New Zealand share market ended the week flat, with brokers reporting increased caution ahead of the October 12 general election.
The top 40 index wound up at 2238.88, down 0.72 on the day and up 15 on last Friday's close.

ANZ Securities' Tim Preston said the market was holding up well in the face of election uncertainty, but more investors were now taking to the sidelines. He said the outlook for the coming week was consequently very quiet.
"There will be flurries of interest, but the trend to the election will be tentative," he said.
